\chapter{La biblioteca que presta cosas}
\label{ch:es-encuesta}
\hlchaptermodality{472}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a report about a service that changed: follow that the idea arose from a survey of its users, that the place is no longer only for reading, and that other places have copied it rather than the other way round.}

Read a report about a library that lends objects, then say where the idea came from and who copied whom.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el usuario]{el usuario — the user}

\label{lesson:ES-C472-usuario}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{usar} and \textbf{la biblioteca}. Today's word is what the second calls the people who do the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el usuario}
\textbf{el usuario} — the user.

\begin{quote}
Preguntaron a los \textbf{usuarios} qué necesitaban.
\end{quote}

\textbf{La usuaria} for a woman. This is the word a library, a transport system or a health service uses for the people it serves, and you will meet it on notices far more often than in speech.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word a service reaches for}]
Spanish picks a different noun depending on what the relationship is, and the choice tells you what kind of place you are in.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the place} & \textbf{what it calls you} \\
\midrule
a shop & \emph{el cliente} — you pay \\
a service & \textbf{el usuario} — you use \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A \emph{biblioteca} has \emph{usuarios}, not \emph{clientes}, because nothing is being sold. A \emph{cliente} implies a transaction; a \emph{usuario} implies \textbf{access}.

So when a notice addresses \emph{los usuarios}, it is telling you something beyond the word: this is a thing you are entitled to use, and the notice expects you to behave accordingly.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{usar} plus \textbf{-ario}, an ending that names the person connected with the thing. Latin \textbf{usus}, a use, from \textbf{uti}, to use.

The same \emph{usus} is inside English \textbf{use}, \textbf{usual} — what is used — and \textbf{utensil}, a thing for using. And \emph{-ario} is the ending in \emph{el bibliotecario}, the librarian, and \emph{el funcionario}, the official.

So \emph{usuario} is transparent once you see it: \textbf{the one who uses}. You could have built it from \emph{usar} the way you built \emph{principiante} from \emph{principio}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item they asked the users what they needed
  \item why a library has \emph{usuarios} and a shop has \emph{clientes}
  \item the verb this word was built from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The user? (\textbf{El usuario}.) Built from? (\textbf{Usar}.) Would a shop use it? (\textbf{No — a shop has clientes}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la encuesta]{la encuesta — the survey}

\label{lesson:ES-C472-encuesta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{preguntar} and \textbf{el usuario}. Do both at once, to a hundred people, and you have today's word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la encuesta}
\textbf{la encuesta} — the survey, the poll.

\begin{quote}
Hicieron una \textbf{encuesta} entre los usuarios.
\end{quote}

\emph{Hacer una encuesta} is the verb it goes with — you \textbf{make} a survey, not \emph{do} one. \emph{Según la encuesta} — according to the survey.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: asking one person and asking a population}]
You already have \emph{preguntar}. An \emph{encuesta} is not more of it — it is a different act.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you do} & \textbf{what you get} \\
\midrule
\textbf{preguntar} & an answer from somebody \\
\textbf{una encuesta} & a picture of what a group thinks \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Preguntar} wants one reply and stops. An \emph{encuesta} is built to be counted, which is why Spanish treats it as a thing you \textbf{make} rather than something you say. That is also why a notice will report \emph{lo que dice la encuesta} — the survey speaks, not the people in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{inquisita}, things sought out, from \textbf{inquirere}: \textbf{in-} plus \textbf{quaerere}, to seek.

Now look at what you already hold. \textbf{Querer} is that same \textbf{quaerere}. The verb that means \emph{to want} in Spanish meant \emph{to seek} in Latin, and \emph{encuesta} is its other child — so \textbf{wanting and asking are one word underneath}, which is truer of people than either word admits on its own.

English took the same root repeatedly: an \textbf{inquest}, an \textbf{inquiry}, a \textbf{question}, a \textbf{quest}, and \textbf{require} — all seekings.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item they made a survey among the users
  \item which taught verb \emph{encuesta} is a cousin of
  \item the difference between \emph{preguntar} and \emph{una encuesta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The survey? (\textbf{La encuesta}.) Which verb goes with it? (\textbf{Hacer}.) Which everyday verb is its cousin? (\textbf{Querer} — both are \emph{quaerere}, to seek.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[surgir]{surgir — to arise}

\label{lesson:ES-C472-surgir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la encuesta} and \textbf{la biblioteca}. An idea came out of the first and changed the second. Today's word is \emph{came out of}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: surgir}
\textbf{surgir} — to arise, to come up, to emerge.

\begin{quote}
La idea \textbf{surgió} de una encuesta.
\end{quote}

\emph{Ha surgido un problema} — a problem has come up. \emph{Surgir de} — to arise \emph{from} something, which is the shape you will meet most.

The \textbf{g} is the throaty one before \emph{i}: \emph{sur-JIR}. Before \emph{a} or \emph{o} it is written \textbf{j} — \emph{surjo}, I arise — so the sound stays put while the spelling moves.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb that reports an origin}]
\emph{Surgir} says something appeared \textbf{without anyone deciding it would}. That is its whole job, and it is why a question about where an idea came from uses it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you say} & \textbf{what it implies} \\
\midrule
la idea \textbf{surgió de} & it emerged, nobody planned it \\
alguien tuvo la idea & a person had it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{¿de dónde surgió la idea?} is not asking who is responsible. It is asking what the idea \textbf{came out of} — a conversation, a complaint, a survey.

Answer it with \emph{de} and a source, the way the question is built.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{surgere}, to rise — itself \textbf{sub-} plus \textbf{regere}, to direct: to straighten oneself up from below.

The picture is physical and the word has kept it. English took the same verb for a \textbf{surge}, a rising of water, and for \textbf{resurgent} and \textbf{insurgent}, things that rise again or rise against.

So \emph{surgir} is not \emph{appear}. It is \textbf{rise}, and what rises came from somewhere underneath — which is exactly why it wants \emph{de}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the idea arose from a survey
  \item a problem has come up
  \item why the word wants \emph{de} after it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To arise? (\textbf{Surgir}.) The idea arose from a survey? (\textbf{La idea surgió de una encuesta}.) What does \emph{surgere} literally mean? (\textbf{To rise}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la lectura]{la lectura — the reading}

\label{lesson:ES-C472-lectura}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{leer} and \textbf{la factura}. One is this word's verb; the other printed this word in a table and moved on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la lectura}
\textbf{la lectura} — the reading.

\begin{quote}
El servicio ya no es solo de \textbf{lectura}.
\end{quote}

You have met this word once without being given it. La factura put it in its own table — \emph{leer, to read | lectura, a reading} — as an example of the \textbf{-ura} ending, then went back to invoices. Here it is as yours.

\emph{Un club de lectura} — a book club. \emph{La lectura del contador} — the meter reading.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three things one word covers}]
English splits these with different words. Spanish keeps one.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what is meant} & \textbf{English reaches for} \\
\midrule
the activity & reading \\
the thing read & a text, a book \\
the interpretation & a reading of \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All three are \emph{la lectura}, and you have already used the third without noticing. When this book asked you for \emph{the two readings of} \textbf{como}, it was asking for two \textbf{lecturas} — two ways the sentence can be taken.

So the word is not only about books. Anything you can take a meaning from has a \emph{lectura}, including a meter and an argument.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Leer} is Latin \textbf{legere}, and \emph{-ura} is the ending \emph{la factura} gave you: the thing an action produces. A \emph{lectura} is what reading makes.

\emph{Legere} first meant \textbf{to gather}, and the reading sense came later — you gather letters the way you gather grain. That gathering is still visible in English \textbf{collect}, \textbf{select} and \textbf{elect}, all of them picking things out, and in \textbf{legible}, able to be gathered, and \textbf{lecture}, a reading aloud.

So the ending was predictable and the root was already yours. The only new thing here is permission to use the word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the service is no longer only for reading
  \item a book club, using today's word
  \item what \emph{legere} first meant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The reading? (\textbf{La lectura}.) Which ending built it? (\textbf{-ura} — the thing an action produces.) What did \emph{legere} first mean? (\textbf{To gather}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[copiar]{copiar — to copy}

\label{lesson:ES-C472-copiar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la lectura} and \textbf{la biblioteca}. If one library's idea works, what do the others do?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: copiar}
\textbf{copiar} — to copy.

\begin{quote}
Tres bibliotecas han \textbf{copiado} el sistema.
\end{quote}

\emph{Copiar un documento}, \emph{copiar a alguien}. The noun is \textbf{la copia}, a copy — and note that it is feminine, where English has no gender to keep track of.

\emph{Copiar en un examen} is to cheat, so the verb is not always neutral; context does the work.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: copying a thing and copying a person}]
The preposition changes what you are claiming.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you say} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
copiar \textbf{el sistema} & reproduce the thing \\
copiar \textbf{a} otra biblioteca & imitate the one who did it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Han copiado el sistema} is a compliment about a method. \emph{Han copiado a otra biblioteca} puts another institution in the sentence and can sound like a charge of unoriginality.

Three libraries copying a system is a success story. The same three copying \emph{a} somebody is a different report altogether, and a reading question will sometimes turn on which one the text said.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{copia} — \textbf{abundance}, plenty. Not \emph{a duplicate}: the word for plenty.

The sense travelled because to copy a manuscript was to make there be \textbf{more of it}. A medieval scribe producing a second manuscript was making \emph{copia}, abundance, and the name of the result eventually became the name of the act.

The old meaning is still in English \textbf{copious}, meaning plentiful, and in \textbf{cornucopia}, the horn of plenty. Set those beside \emph{una copia} and the journey is visible: from having a lot, to having another one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item three libraries have copied the system
  \item the difference \emph{a} makes after this verb
  \item what \emph{copia} meant in Latin
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To copy? (\textbf{Copiar}.) The noun? (\textbf{La copia} — feminine.) What did \emph{copia} mean first? (\textbf{Abundance}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(el usuario, la encuesta, surgir, la …]{(el usuario, la encuesta, surgir, la lectura, copiar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R472-repaso-encuesta}



\begin{quote}
Five words, no prompts. Who the library serves, what it asked them, what came out of it, what the place used to be only for, and what the neighbours did next.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the five, cold}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
the user & \textbf{el usuario} \\
the survey & \textbf{la encuesta} \\
to arise & \textbf{surgir} \\
the reading & \textbf{la lectura} \\
to copy & \textbf{copiar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three of the five were already inside words you hold}]
This chapter minted very little. Most of it was recombination.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it is made of} \\
\midrule
usuario & \textbf{usar} plus \emph{-ario} \\
lectura & \textbf{leer} plus \emph{-ura} \\
encuesta & the same Latin verb as \textbf{querer} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La factura} had even printed \emph{lectura} in a table already, as its own example of the \emph{-ura} ending, and moved on. So the work here was less learning words than being handed ones the book had been using in front of you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The two that were genuinely new both hide a picture.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{underneath} \\
\midrule
surgir & \emph{surgere}, to \textbf{rise} — so it wants \emph{de} \\
copiar & \emph{copia}, \textbf{abundance} — a copy made there be more \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And the one worth keeping: \textbf{encuesta} is \emph{inquirere}, \textbf{in-} plus \emph{quaerere}, to seek — and \emph{quaerere} is \textbf{querer}. Wanting and asking are the same Latin verb, which is a better joke than either language intended.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the idea arose from a survey among the users
  \item three libraries have copied the system
  \item which two of the five you could have built yourself
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The user? (\textbf{El usuario}.) The survey? (\textbf{La encuesta}.) To arise? (\textbf{Surgir}.) The reading? (\textbf{La lectura}.) To copy? (\textbf{Copiar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(la biblioteca que presta cosas) — read it, then answer}

\label{lesson:ES-C472-sintesis-encuesta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la encuesta} and \textbf{surgir}. The question below joins those two words, and it is the only question in this chapter you have to answer.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
La biblioteca ya no presta solo libros. Desde hace dos años presta también objetos: herramientas, maletas, máquinas de cocina.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La idea \textbf{surgió} de una \textbf{encuesta}: preguntaron a los \textbf{usuarios} qué necesitaban y qué no querían comprar. El servicio dejó de ser solo de \textbf{lectura} y tres bibliotecas de la provincia ya lo han \textbf{copiado}.
\end{quote}
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question is about the source, not the author}]
An exam will ask \textbf{¿de dónde surgió la idea?} and offer three answers. Two of them will be plausible-sounding origins the text does not claim.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what the text says} & \textbf{what it does not say} \\
\midrule
surgió \textbf{de una encuesta} & that somebody proposed it \\
otras bibliotecas \textbf{lo han copiado} & that this one copied another \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That second row is the trap worth naming. The text says other libraries copied \textbf{this} one. A distractor will offer the reverse — \emph{de copiar otra biblioteca} — and it uses the chapter's own word to do it.

\emph{Surgir de} points \textbf{backwards} to a source. Read the direction as carefully as the words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say where the idea came from, using \emph{surgir de}.

Now say who copied whom, in that order, and then say it the wrong way round so you can hear the difference.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did the idea come from? (\textbf{De una encuesta}.) Who was asked? (\textbf{Los usuarios}.) Who copied whom? (\textbf{Otras bibliotecas copiaron a esta}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
